impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that licenses exclusive commercialization rights but retains the right to sue third parties for infringement has sufficient constitutional standing to bring an infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who retains an exclusionary right to sue for infringement—even after granting an exclusive license to manufacture and sell—retains sufficient injury-in-fact to satisfy Article III standing. The court found the retained right to sue was not rendered illusory by the rights granted to the licensee.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring licensing agreements can retain standing to enforce patents against third parties by carefully preserving the right to sue for infringement, even when granting broad exclusive licenses.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers may face suits from patent owners who have licensed away most commercial rights, making it harder to challenge standing as a defense strategy.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting JMOL that Teva's headache patents claiming humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity, reinstating the jury's findings that Eli Lilly willfully infringed Teva's patents covering use of humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for headache treatment and that the patents were not invalid. This decision has major implications for the blockbuster migraine drug market involving CGRP-targeting antibodies.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical patent holders benefit from the court's willingness to uphold genus claims for antibody patents where the specification discloses known methods for making the claimed antibodies, protecting broad patent coverage for biologic drugs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitors developing CGRP-targeting antibody therapies face renewed infringement risk, and the decision may limit challenges to broad biologic patent claims under § 112.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied IPR estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar Valve from asserting invalidity grounds that were not raised in a prior IPR petition but allegedly could have been discovered through a reasonably diligent search.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against Valve on two invalidity grounds, finding insufficient evidence to support estoppel on one ground and inadequate consideration of hindsight bias on the other. The decision clarifies the evidentiary standards for determining what a 'skilled searcher' conducting a 'diligent search' reasonably could have discovered.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent litigation benefit from a higher evidentiary bar for IPR estoppel, preserving their ability to raise invalidity defenses in district court even after filing IPR petitions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face a more difficult path to invoking IPR estoppel to foreclose invalidity defenses, potentially increasing the cost and complexity of patent enforcement.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. Ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in its jury instructions and verdict form regarding patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 and whether a single verdict question covering infringement of multiple patents warranted a new trial.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgments and remanded for a new trial, finding that the verdict form's use of a single infringement question covering all four asserted patents was reversible error. The court also remanded for further proceedings under Alice step two for the '495 patent while affirming eligibility of other patents directed to wireless building automation systems.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent defendants benefit from the requirement that verdict forms must allow juries to make separate infringement findings for each asserted patent, preventing potentially inflated aggregate damages awards.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders pursuing multi-patent infringement cases face increased procedural requirements for verdict forms, potentially complicating trial strategy and increasing litigation costs.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using passive data collection devices on farming equipment are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in finding the case was not exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's asserted patent claims relating to farming data collection and sharing were directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas under § 101, but vacated and remanded the district court's finding that the case was not exceptional, potentially opening the door to attorney fee awards. The decision reinforces that data collection and processing claims in agriculture technology may face § 101 challenges.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies accused of infringing data-collection patents in agriculture and similar industries can leverage § 101 as a defense, and may recover fees if such cases are found exceptional.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies holding patents on data-driven agricultural technology face heightened invalidation risk under § 101 and potential fee exposure if their enforcement efforts are deemed exceptional.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to support the jury's finding that each of the asserted trade secrets qualified as a protectable trade secret under California law.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims involving a cosmetic penile implant, finding insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying information was generally known. The court also reversed on patent inventorship, vacated exemplary damages and the permanent injunction, but affirmed liability on a counterfeiting claim.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret litigation benefit from rigorous appellate review of whether asserted information truly qualifies as a trade secret, preventing overreach by plaintiffs claiming protection for generally known information.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret protection must ensure robust evidence that their claimed secrets are not generally known in the industry, or risk reversal of favorable verdicts and injunctions.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act had expired before Insulet brought suit alleging that EOFlow misappropriated trade secrets relating to its Omnipod insulin patch pump.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's denial of JMOL, holding that Insulet's DTSA claim was time-barred because the statute of limitations had expired before suit was filed. Despite a jury verdict finding misappropriation and awarding damages, the court determined that Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing. This decision underscores the critical importance of timely filing in trade secret cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation can invoke the statute of limitations as a powerful defense, particularly where the plaintiff had constructive or actual knowledge of the alleged misappropriation well before filing suit.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret holders must act promptly upon discovering or having reason to know of misappropriation, as delays beyond the statutory period will bar recovery regardless of the merits of the underlying claim.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding plaintiff's damages expert testimony and in its determination of damages for trade secret misappropriation and breach of contract related to automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the district court's reduction of breach of contract damages and reinstated the jury's original award, while affirming Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation under both the DTSA and Michigan law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software developers and licensors benefit from the court's instruction that multiple damages models should be considered in trade secret cases, and from reinstatement of jury contract damages awards.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop in-house alternatives to licensed software face ongoing misappropriation liability and potentially larger damages exposure on remand.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit partially vacated the district court's summary judgment of patent eligibility, finding that certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents required further analysis under the Alice framework, while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents. The court also affirmed the denial of JMOL on infringement and damages, including the admissibility of damages expert testimony. The case involves patents central to digital TV broadcast standards.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology standard implementers benefit from the court's willingness to scrutinize § 101 eligibility of claims incorporated into communication standards, potentially reducing royalty obligations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders with claims incorporated into industry standards face renewed eligibility challenges, and partial vacatur creates uncertainty about the scope of enforceable patent rights.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly granted summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and rejection of a doctrine of equivalents theory, and whether it properly struck damages expert theories for inadequate disclosure.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part the grant of summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's '836 patent relating to multicore processor task allocation, finding genuine issues of material fact remained. The court addressed the extraterritorial reach of U.S. patent law in the context of globally manufactured semiconductor chips. The decision was affirmed in part regarding certain damages theory exclusions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting infringement of semiconductor and processor patents benefit from the court's narrowing of the extraterritoriality defense, preserving claims against chips designed or partially manufactured abroad.
impacts.negativeImplications: Semiconductor manufacturers face renewed infringement exposure for multicore processor designs, and the decision creates uncertainty about the territorial scope of patent liability for globally distributed manufacturing processes.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative testimony is admissible at summary judgment even when the witness lacks personal knowledge, and whether computer source code constitutes hearsay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the pre-AIA on-sale bar, holding that Rule 30(b)(6) testimony is admissible even when the corporate representative joined the company after the relevant events, and that computer source code describing commands is not hearsay. The court rejected the argument that the on-sale bar should be limited to sales expressly disclosing a device's functionality.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from expanded evidentiary tools at summary judgment, including broader admissibility of corporate representative testimony and source code, strengthening prior art defenses.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face a broader on-sale bar that does not require express disclosure of device functionality in prior sales, and may have difficulty challenging corporate deposition testimony on personal knowledge grounds.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) by voluntarily dismissing a first-filed declaratory judgment action where it missed the statutory deadline and then refiling a new action to reset the clock.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the mandatory stay deadline under § 1659(a)(2) by dismissing and refiling a declaratory judgment action. BioMarin had missed the 30-day deadline in the original action and attempted to file a new DJ action to obtain a fresh stay period. The court found this gamesmanship impermissible under the statute.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical and life sciences companies filing DJ actions benefit from certainty that ITC respondents cannot manipulate the mandatory stay mechanism through serial refiling of complaints.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the § 1659(a)(2) deadline lose the ability to obtain a mandatory stay of parallel district court proceedings, potentially forcing them to litigate on two fronts simultaneously.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to pH measured at a standard temperature in the field, and whether the patent holder was barred from asserting infringement by equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding of no literal infringement of Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents, agreeing that the claim term 'pH of 13 or higher' refers to pH measured at a standard temperature. The court also upheld the ruling barring Actelion from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents. This decision impacts the generic drug market for pulmonary hypertension treatments.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical manufacturers benefit from clear claim construction standards for pharmaceutical composition patents, facilitating ANDA-based generic drug development.
impacts.negativeImplications: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies face narrower patent protection when claims use scientific measurements that are temperature-dependent, potentially allowing generic competitors to design around patents.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an entity that was not served in the underlying district court litigation but filed an IPR petition on the same day as the statutory deadline for the actual defendant is time-barred under 35 U.S.C. § 315(b), and whether the Board's obviousness determination was supported by substantial evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness determination invalidating FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded for further proceedings. The court also addressed concerns about a non-party (Qualcomm) filing an IPR petition on the same day as the actual defendant's (Roambee's) statutory deadline, raising questions about real-party-in-interest and privity issues under § 315(b).
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from greater scrutiny of IPR petitions filed by entities that appear to be acting as surrogates for time-barred parties, protecting against potential abuse of the IPR system.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies seeking to challenge competitor patents through IPR face heightened scrutiny when their petitions coincide with statutory deadlines for related parties, potentially limiting strategic use of the IPR process.

impacts.caseName: mCom IP, LLC v. City National Bank of Florida
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may dismiss a patent infringement complaint with prejudice based on obviousness grounds previously established in an IPR against related claims, and whether attorney fees under § 285 and sanctions under § 1927 were warranted.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed dismissal of mCom's patent infringement complaint on obviousness grounds but reversed the exceptional-case fee award under § 285 and attorney sanctions under § 1927, finding that the grounds presented were insufficient to support exceptionality or bad faith. The decision clarifies the interplay between IPR outcomes and subsequent district court litigation on surviving claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders whose claims survive IPR benefit from the court's higher bar for exceptional-case findings and attorney sanctions, protecting their right to enforce surviving claims without fee risk.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies asserting patents where related claims were invalidated in IPR remain vulnerable to dismissal on the same grounds, even for claims not directly challenged in the IPR proceeding.
